text: Attackers can bypass application logic on dual-use endpoints by omitting mandatory parameters. When multiple operations are handled by a single controller or script, parameter presence acts as an implicit router. Deleting a parameter name or its value can force the backend into unhandled fallback routines, alternative code branches, or privilege escalation paths.

metadata.title: Parameter Omission and Dual-Use Endpoint Exploitation
metadata.technique: Systematic parameter removal across GET, POST, and Cookie headers
execution_steps: Intercept request using an HTTP proxy
Remove one parameter at a time (both key and value)
Submit and inspect response diffs for fallback routing
Trace multi-stage workflows to identify state desynchronization

text: Forced browsing and step skipping in multi-stage workflows allow attackers to reach terminal states without satisfying intermediate requirements. For instance, in two-factor authentication (Login -> 2FA Prompt -> Account Dashboard), directly invoking the post-2FA endpoint via forced browsing circumvents token submission when the server relies on client navigation order instead of server-side state enforcement.

metadata.title: State Sequence Violation and Workflow Step-Skipping
metadata.flawed_assumption: Users will sequentially advance through pages in the order dictated by the client interface.
associated_labs: Authentication bypass via flawed state machine (Practitioner)

text: In e-commerce workflows, state desynchronization occurs when cart adjustment calculations do not recalculate discounts after cart modification. An attacker adds items to exceed a discount threshold (e.g., $1000 for 10% off), applies the coupon, and subsequently removes the items; if the server fails to verify preconditions upon checkout, the discount persists on the smaller total.

metadata.title: State Desynchronization in Post-Condition Order Discounts

rule_constraints.invariant: cart.subtotal >= 1000 must hold at checkout execution

metadata.vulnerability_mechanism: Missing re-validation of pricing invariants when cart mutation occurs in intermediate state.

text: In a purchasing workflow, the client browser transmits the item unit price directly within the POST request payload when adding items to the cart. Because the server fails to validate the price against a database source of truth, an attacker intercepting the request can manipulate the price parameter to an arbitrary low value (e.g., less than available store credit), enabling checkout completion without adequate funds.

metadata.title: Arbitrary Price Tampering via Client-Supplied Parameter
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
attack_steps: Authenticate with standard credentials.
Attempt order to determine insufficient credit ceiling.
Intercept 'POST /cart' request containing client-specified 'price' parameter.
Tamper 'price' value to an arbitrary lower integer within balance limit.
Submit order via checkout endpoint to complete purchase.

text: Pattern: Transaction Total Manipulation via Negative Item Quantities. In an e-commerce purchasing workflow, an add-to-cart or cart-update endpoint accepts user-controlled item quantities without validating that the integer is strictly positive. When a negative quantity is supplied, the application performs signed arithmetic on both the line item and total order calculations (item_total = price * quantity). An attacker can add an expensive target item to the cart, then add a calculated negative quantity of another product to reduce the overall order subtotal to an arbitrary low or negative value, bypassing store credit or balance limits during checkout. Example Trace: Intercept POST /cart, submit 'productId=2' with 'quantity=-10' alongside the target high-value product, reducing the cart subtotal below available store credit, and execute checkout.

metadata.title: Cart Subtotal Reduction via Negative Quantity Injection
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-1284: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input
attack_steps: Authenticate with standard buyer credentials.
Add expensive target item (e.g., leather jacket) to cart.
Intercept cart addition request for a secondary item.
Inject a negative integer value into the quantity parameter.
Verify that the subtotal is reduced by (unit_price * |negative_quantity|).
Balance the equation so 0 < total_price <= user_credit.
Complete checkout.

text: Pattern: Inconsistent Security Controls via Post-Registration Identity Mutation. The application restricts privileged functionality (e.g., administrative panels) based on user email domain matching. While initial account registration enforces domain restrictions or requires domain verification (e.g., email confirmation links), secondary account management workflows (such as updating profile email) lack the same domain validation or re-verification controls. An attacker registers with an arbitrary permitted domain, updates their email address to a privileged domain (e.g., @company.com) via user settings, and bypasses administrative access barriers.

metadata.title: Privilege Escalation via Inconsistent Email Domain Verification
attack_steps: Enumerate restricted/admin interfaces to identify access requirements or privileged domains from error messages.
Register a standard account using a legitimate/controllable domain and complete email activation.
Authenticate and navigate to secondary profile update functionality.
Update account email address directly to the privileged target domain (e.g., victim-corp.com) without undergoing re-verification.
Access restricted administrative endpoints with elevated privileges.
Execute administrative actions (e.g., user deletion).

concrete_example.mutation_action: Update email to @dontwannacry.com via account settings

text: Pattern: Coupon Replay via State History Naivety (Alternating Code Application). In checkout workflows, an application enforces single-use constraints on promotional discount coupons by only comparing incoming coupon submissions against the most recently applied coupon code (last_applied_coupon != current_coupon) rather than maintaining an aggregated set or transaction-level redemption ledger. An attacker alternates submissions between two or more valid coupon codes (e.g., CODE_A -> CODE_B -> CODE_A -> CODE_B), repeatedly resetting the immediate state check and compounding discounts until the order total is reduced to an arbitrary low value or zero.

metadata.title: Compounded Discount Abuse via Alternating Coupon Application
attack_steps: Acquire multiple distinct promotional discount codes.
Add target items to cart.
Submit first coupon code (e.g., POST /cart/coupon with NEWCUST5).
Attempt duplicate submission of same code to confirm immediate rejection.
Submit alternate coupon code (e.g., SIGNUP30).
Alternately resubmit both codes in sequence (A -> B -> A -> B) to continuously depress order total below available credit.
Complete checkout order.

text: Pattern: Financial Total Manipulation via 32-Bit Signed Integer Overflow. An application enforces superficial limits on input quantity parameters (e.g., maximum 2-digit integer per request), but fails to enforce upper bounds or overflow protections on the cumulative cart balance stored in primitive integer types (such as a 32-bit signed int, INT_MAX = 2,147,483,647 cents). An attacker repeatedly dispatches item addition requests (e.g., quantity=99) using automated request flooding. Once cumulative total exceeds INT_MAX, the variable wraps around to the negative boundary (INT_MIN = -2,147,483,648). The attacker precisely calculates payload iterations and auxiliary item offsets to settle the wrapped subtotal into a valid positive range below available store credit, completing checkout below true cost.

metadata.title: Integer Overflow in Financial Aggregation Logic
attack_steps: Identify per-request quantity input validation ceiling (e.g., 2-digit ceiling).
Observe total financial value representation (e.g., stored internally in cents).
Utilize automated request generation (e.g., Burp Intruder Null Payloads) with serial concurrency (pool=1) to increment line items toward 32-bit signed limit (2,147,483,647).
Verify integer wraparound occurs when total flips to negative boundary (-2,147,483,648).
Calculate required payload count to settle wrapped negative balance near zero.
Inject auxiliary item quantities to offset negative balance into the target payable window ($0 < total <= balance).
Submit order checkout to acquire target products.

text: Pattern: Privilege Escalation via String Truncation Discrepancy (Database Storage vs Validation Layer). An application uses the recipient email address for two distinct operations: sending out-of-band account activation tokens via SMTP, and evaluating user domain authorization in the administrative access controller. The validation and mail-routing layers support long email strings without length enforcement, while the database storage layer silently truncates strings exceeding a fixed column capacity (e.g., VARCHAR(255)). An attacker constructs a crafted email address where the subdomain segment matches the privileged corporate domain (e.g., prefix@target-corp.com.attacker-domain.tld) padded precisely so the 255th character aligns with the end of the corporate domain. The email server routes the activation token to the attacker's full domain, while database persistence clips the attacker's trailing domain, converting the stored identity into a verified corporate user with administrative access.

metadata.title: Privilege Escalation via Email Truncation and Domain Boundary Clipping
metadata.state_transition: UNREGISTERED -> REGISTRATION_SUBMITTED (Long String) -> TOKEN_DELIVERED (Full Domain) -> ACCOUNT_PERSISTED (Truncated Domain) -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED
attack_steps: Probe registration with an oversized email address (>200 chars) to observe storage behavior on profile reflection.
Identify storage boundary truncation (e.g., string sliced at exactly 255 characters).
Calculate padding length: prefix_len + len('@privileged-domain.com') == truncation_limit (255).
Construct payload: [padding]@[privileged-domain.com].[attacker-controlled-domain].
Submit registration; activation email routes to attacker control via full DNS hierarchy.
Complete verification via confirmation link.
Authenticate to verify stored email clipped to target domain (@privileged-domain.com).
Access administrative panel and invoke privileged actions.

text: Pattern: Privilege Escalation via Parameter Omission on Dual-Use Endpoints. A single backend controller handles password modification for both self-service user updates and administrative overrides. The application relies on the presence of the 'current-password' parameter to infer whether the caller is a standard user (requiring existing credential validation) or an administrator (bypassing verification). Additionally, the target user identity is derived from a client-controllable 'username' parameter rather than strictly binding to the authenticated session context. An attacker removes the 'current-password' parameter entirely and overrides the 'username' parameter with a privileged account (e.g., 'administrator'), causing the backend to execute the administrative override branch and overwrite the target account's password without prior authentication.

metadata.title: Arbitrary Password Reset via Dual-Use Endpoint Parameter Omission
metadata.state_transition: AUTHENTICATED_LOW_PRIV -> DISPATCH_DUAL_USE_ACTION (Omitted Verification Param + Mutated Target Identity) -> TARGET_ACCOUNT_COMPROMISED -> PRIVILEGED_SESSION_ACQUIRED
attack_steps: Authenticate with low-privilege credentials and perform a baseline password change.
Inspect the HTTP request (e.g., POST /my-account/change-password).
Observe dual-use parameters: 'username', 'current-password', and 'new-password-1'.
Omit the 'current-password' parameter entirely to test for execution branch switching.
Verify that password change succeeds without current credential validation.
Inject a target high-privilege account identifier into 'username' (e.g., username=administrator).
Submit the request and authenticate as the targeted user using the newly established password.

text: Pattern: Forced Browsing and Workflow Step-Skipping in Purchasing Checkout. The purchasing state machine improperly assumes that navigating to the terminal confirmation endpoint can only occur after successful payment settlement. The server-side fulfillment handler evaluates the GET /cart/order-confirmation?order-confirmation=true request as an authoritative completion trigger rather than verifying that the active session's cart successfully completed the transactional payment stage (e.g., POST /cart/checkout). An attacker populates the cart with high-value items and directly replays the order-confirmation request, completing order fulfillment without initiating the payment or deduction routine.

metadata.title: Purchasing Workflow Step-Skipping via Direct Confirmation Invocations
attack_steps: Complete a baseline purchase of an affordable item to map normal workflow progression.
Inspect proxy history and record terminal confirmation request (e.g., GET /cart/order-confirmation?order-confirmation=true).
Add targeted high-value item to the cart.
Bypass intermediate payment submission endpoints entirely using forced browsing to directly issue the recorded confirmation request.
Verify that the order moves to confirmed state without financial balance deduction.

text: Pattern: Authentication Bypass via Partial Workflow Abort / State Machine Dropping. An application implements a multi-step authentication flow: credential verification followed by intermediate role assignment (POST /login -> GET /role-selector -> POST /role-selector -> Home). The backend initializes the session state with an implicit or unconstrained privileged role (e.g., admin) immediately upon credential verification, assuming the subsequent role-selector step will safely downgrade or explicitly set the user's intended role. By intercepting and dropping the intermediate transition request (GET /role-selector) and navigating directly to the application core, the attacker halts workflow progression before the unprivileged role assignment takes place, retaining the default elevated state.

metadata.title: Authentication Bypass and Privilege Default via Dropped State Transition
metadata.state_transition: UNAUTHENTICATED -> CREDENTIALS_VALIDATED (Default State: Admin) -> [GET /role-selector DROPPED] -> ROLE_INITIALIZATION_ABORTED -> PRIVILEGED_DASHBOARD_ACCESSED
attack_steps: Authenticate with baseline unprivileged credentials (wiener:peter) and map multi-step login sequence.
Identify role-selection intermediate state (/role-selector) preceding landing dashboard.
Identify restricted administration paths (e.g., /admin) via content discovery.
Re-authenticate while intercepting traffic in an HTTP proxy.
Forward initial credential submission (POST /login).
Intercept and drop the follow-up intermediate request (GET /role-selector).
Directly browse to the target root / home page using the active session.
Verify session inherits default unconstrained administrative role and execute admin actions.

text: Pattern: Infinite Currency Arbitrage via Reusable Discount on Cash-Equivalent Instruments. An application permits generic promotional discount codes (e.g., 30% off) to apply to cash-equivalent instruments such as gift cards or store vouchers. When a user purchases a gift card of face value $V at discounted cost $C (where C < V) using store credit and subsequently redeems the newly issued voucher into the same store credit balance, the net account balance increases by (V - C) per cycle. By chaining this loop within an automated macro or concurrency runner (Cart Addition -> Apply Discount -> Checkout -> Extract Issued Voucher -> Redeem Voucher), an attacker generates unbounded store credit without introducing external capital.

metadata.title: Infinite Store Credit Generation via Discounted Gift Card Arbitrage
metadata.state_transition: INITIAL_BALANCE -> GIFT_CARD_PURCHASE_DISCOUNTED -> ORDER_FULFILLED -> VOUCHER_REDEEMED -> INFLATED_BALANCE -> LOOP_REPEAT
attack_steps: Acquire reusable or self-service promotional coupon (e.g., SIGNUP30 granting 30% discount).
Add cash-equivalent item (e.g., $10 gift card) to shopping cart.
Apply discount coupon to reduce checkout total below card face value ($7 instead of $10).
Complete purchase using current store credit.
Extract issued gift card code from fulfillment response (GET /cart/order-confirmation).
Submit redemption request (POST /gift-card) to credit full face value ($10) back to account balance.
Automate the multi-step cycle via macro/script to compound store credit iteratively until targeted financial ceiling is met.

text: Pattern: Authentication Bypass via Dual Encryption/Decryption Oracle and Ciphertext Manipulation. An application reuses identical cryptographic keys, algorithms, and block-cipher modes across distinct functional domains (e.g., transient UI notifications and persistent authentication session cookies). When an unhandled error path reflects decrypted user input (decryption oracle via notification cookie) and a validation failure path returns encrypted user input in a cookie (encryption oracle via email error handler), an attacker decrypts their legitimate session token to identify its structural schema (e.g., username:timestamp). The attacker then encrypts an arbitrary target payload (administrator:timestamp). Because the application prefixes error inputs with static text ('Invalid email address: '), the attacker pads the payload so the prefix and padding align to cipher block boundaries (e.g., 16-byte blocks in CBC/ECB mode). Slicing off the initial 32 bytes of ciphertext eliminates the prefix without invalidating the trailing target ciphertext block, forging a valid persistent administrator session token.

metadata.title: Authentication Cookie Forgery via Symmetric Encryption Oracle and Block Truncation
metadata.state_transition: AUTHENTICATED_LOW_PRIV -> ORACLE_KEY_REUSE_DISCOVERED -> CIPHERTEXT_DECRYPTED (Schema Extracted) -> PADDED_TARGET_ENCRYPTED -> CIPHER_BLOCK_SLICED -> ADMIN_SESSION_FORGED -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED
attack_steps: Log in with persistent session enabled ('Stay logged in') and capture the encrypted 'stay-logged-in' cookie.
Submit invalid input into a secondary endpoint (e.g., invalid email in comment form) to trigger error tracking via encrypted 'notification' cookie.
Observe that retrieving the target post decrypts the 'notification' cookie and reflects the plaintext string, establishing a decryption oracle.
Feed 'stay-logged-in' ciphertext into the 'notification' parameter to decrypt the token and discover its format: username:timestamp.
Note that the encryption oracle prepends a 23-byte static prefix ('Invalid email address: ').
Calculate block alignment padding: 23 bytes prefix + 9 padding bytes = 32 bytes (exact multiple of 16-byte block cipher).
Submit padded payload (xxxxxxxxxadministrator:timestamp) to the encryption oracle (email parameter) and capture the resulting ciphertext.
Decode Base64 ciphertext, remove the first 32 bytes (2 cipher blocks), re-encode to Base64, and verify via decryption oracle that only 'administrator:timestamp' remains.
Replace 'stay-logged-in' cookie with the forged ciphertext to authenticate as administrator and access privileged endpoints.

text: Pattern: Access Control and Domain Validation Bypass via Email Encoded-Word (RFC 2047) Parser Discrepancy. An application restricts user registration and administrative privileges to an authoritative internal domain (e.g., ginandjuice.shop) by inspecting the trailing domain substring of incoming email addresses. The front-end validation layer detects common MIME Encoded-Word formats (e.g., =?iso-8859-1?q?...?= and =?utf-8?q?...?=) but fails to blacklist or normalize legacy encodings such as UTF-7 (RFC 1642 / RFC 2152, =?utf-7?q?...?=). An attacker crafts an email payload embedding their actual external address and delimiter characters inside an unhandled UTF-7 encoded-word block while affixing the required corporate domain as an external suffix: =?utf-7?q?attacker&AEA-[EXPLOIT_HOST]&ACA-?=@target-corp.com. The registration validation check interprets the trailing unencoded @target-corp.com as compliant, whereas the underlying downstream mail-transfer agent (MTA) or SMTP client decodes the embedded UTF-7 delimiter (&AEA- -> @, &ACA- -> space) and routes the out-of-band activation token to the attacker-controlled server. Upon link verification, the backend derives privileged access based on the verified corporate domain identity.

metadata.title: Registration Domain Bypass via RFC 2047 UTF-7 MIME Encoding Discrepancy
metadata.state_transition: UNAUTHENTICATED -> ENCODED_REGISTRATION_SUBMITTED (UTF-7 Encoded Delimiters) -> DOMAIN_CHECK_PASSED -> OUT_OF_BAND_TOKEN_ROUTED_ATTACKER -> ACCOUNT_ACTIVATED -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED
attack_steps: Submit baseline registration using an unauthorized external domain to identify target domain constraints from the failure response.
Test encoded-word MIME encapsulation using standard charsets (=?iso-8859-1?=, =?utf-8?=) to detect security filter signatures.
Identify filter discrepancy by injecting legacy charsets (e.g., =?utf-7?=) that evade the pattern-matching filter without triggering rejection.
Encode the attacker's delivery domain and separator characters into UTF-7 representation (&AEA- for '@', &ACA- for space).
Append the mandatory corporate domain as the outer unencoded suffix: =?utf-7?q?attacker&AEA-[EXPLOIT_HOST]&ACA-?=@target-domain.com.
Submit registration; confirm that out-of-band activation email arrives at the attacker's mail server via decoded MTA routing.
Activate the account using the confirmation link and log in to inherit privileged administrative rights.

text: Overview of Email Atom Splitting and Parser Discrepancies: Email parsing standards (RFC 2822 / RFC 5322) incorporate complex behaviors including quoted local-parts, comments, escape sequences, and multi-layer MIME encodings (e.g., encoded-words, Punycode, UUCP, and source routes). Because web applications farm out email validation and parsing to diverse libraries without knowing how downstream mail transfer agents (MTAs) interpret the input, discrepancies arise. Attackers exploit these gaps to route emails to unexpected destinations, bypass domain-based access controls on platforms like GitHub, Zendesk, and GitLab, or trigger code execution vulnerabilities such as style tag injection and CSS exfiltration leading to RCE in Joomla (CVE-2024-21725).

metadata.title: Splitting the Email Atom: Exploiting Parsers to Bypass Access Controls
metadata.impact: Access Control Bypass, Cloudflare Zero Trust IdP Impersonation, and Remote Code Execution via CSS Exfiltration.

text: Pattern: Email Domain Confusion via Archaic Protocol Invocations. Email routing parsers and mailers (such as Sendmail and Postfix) inherit support for legacy protocols predating modern internet standards, including UUCP (Unix To Unix Copy, using exclamation mark separators) and source-chaining percent hacks/source routes. By injecting escape characters, double quotes, and archaic separators (e.g., ! or %), an attacker creates confusion between the validation layer and the underlying mail transfer agent. This causes the application validation layer to treat the address as belonging to an allowed domain while the mailer routes the message or out-of-band verification token to an attacker-controlled external mail server.

metadata.title: Email Domain Confusion via UUCP and Source Routes

text: Pattern: Email Splitting via MIME Encoded-Word (RFC 2047). Applications relying on libraries like Ruby's 'Mail' gem parse and decode RFC 2047 encoded-word sequences (=?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=) within email addresses. Attackers encode characters such as raw at-symbols (=40), command termination characters (=3e for greater-than), and null bytes (=00) to terminate SMTP commands prematurely or inject secondary mailbox destinations. This passes front-end domain regex validation while splitting the recipient specification during MTA transmission, allowing attackers to forge verified domain ownership on platforms like GitHub, Zendesk, and GitLab.

metadata.title: Email Splitting via MIME Encoded-Word Discrepancies

text: Pattern: Remote Code Execution via Punycode Malformation and CSS Exfiltration (CVE-2024-21725). Defective PHP IDN libraries mishandle malformed Punycode sequences containing non-standard digit combinations (e.g., xn--0049, xn--42), decoding them into unintended characters like opening angle brackets and style tags. When output in vulnerable applications like Joomla, this injects an unclosed HTML style tag into user list pages. An attacker registers two accounts: the first injects the malicious Punycode domain opening a style tag, and the second injects CSS import statements using curly braces to neutralize subsequent HTML. Combined with a custom CSS exfiltration tool, this steals super administrator CSRF tokens, enabling automated modification of backend templates to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE).

metadata.title: RCE via Punycode Malformation, Style Injection, and CSS Exfiltration in Joomla
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
attack_steps: Identify IDN library decoding flaw in PHP application
Register account 1 with malformed Punycode generating unclosed HTML style tags
Register account 2 containing CSS import rules and curly braces to neutralize trailing HTML
Harvest administrator CSRF token via blind CSS exfiltration stylesheet
Forge administrative request to edit backend PHP template and achieve RCE
